addressed_problems.content: Extending Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) beyond depth scaling remains an unresolved challenge. The current Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH) supports only depth-wise stretching and squeezing within a single architectural design family (e.g., ResNets, VGGs). Preliminary attempts to apply ETTs to width transformations (e.g., replicating or dropping filters/channels) encountered significantly greater difficulty and degraded performance. Consequently, a method for transferring winning tickets across networks that differ in width, or that undergo mixed topological changes (simultaneous depth, width, and connectivity alterations), has not been established. Resolving this limitation is necessary to generalize E-LTH to the full range of architecture variations encountered in practice, such as scaling along multiple dimensions or transferring across fundamentally different families (e.g., ResNet to Transformer).

A rigorous theoretical foundation for the Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH) is lacking. The paper provides two intuitive perspectives—the dynamical systems interpretation (each residual block as a time step in ODE discretization) and the unrolled estimation interpretation (successive blocks refine a latent representation)—but these are explicitly acknowledged as preliminary hypotheses that are largely restricted to ResNet architectures. They do not constitute a general theory that explains why replicating or dropping layers from a source winning ticket preserves the trainability of the resulting sparse mask in a target network. Without such a theory, the conditions under which mask replication or removal succeeds remain empirical, and the observed transferability cannot be reliably predicted or extended to novel architectural changes.

Producing high-quality winning tickets with structured sparsity (e.g., channel-level pruning) that are hardware-friendly remains an open problem. The current lottery ticket literature, including E-LTH, relies on unstructured sparsity and iterative magnitude pruning (IMP). While structured sparsity offers better acceleration on conventional hardware, state-of-the-art methods for structured lottery tickets (e.g., Early-Bird tickets via channel pruning) sacrifice significant accuracy compared to unstructured LTH. The paper explicitly notes that finding a high-quality lottery ticket with structured sparsity is 'an open and unsolved question' and is beyond the scope of the work. Addressing this gap is important for bridging LTH research with practical deployment on hardware that benefits from structured patterns.

A precise definition of 'architectural similarity' that determines when winning tickets are transferable between networks is unresolved. E-LTH currently assumes that target and source architectures belong to the same 'design family' (e.g., series of models with repeating blocks and same stage counts), but no formal criterion exists to decide whether two arbitrary architectures share transferable sparse patterns. The paper suggests leveraging relational graph representations of neural networks (e.g., [45]) to explore a broader design space, but this remains future work. Without a quantitative measure of architectural similarity, it is unclear how far E-LTH can generalize beyond the specific family (ResNet, VGG) and depth transformations tested.

Understanding the loss-basin relationships that govern the success or failure of ticket transfer is an open question. The paper observes that linear mode connectivity (LMC)—the property that two solutions can be linearly interpolated without accuracy loss—holds for transferred tickets when source and target networks differ modestly in depth (e.g., ResNet-20 to ResNet-32) but degrades significantly when the depth gap is large (e.g., ResNet-14 to ResNet-32). This suggests that the transferred ticket may or may not lie in the same basin as a directly found IMP ticket. Characterizing the safe range of architectural transformations (e.g., maximum number of layers added or removed) that preserve basin membership, and understanding the relationship between basin structure and transferability, are necessary to provide principled guidance for reliable ticket transfer.

Modern "lottery ticket" research seeks sparse subnetworks ("winning tickets") that can be trained in isolation to match dense models. The standard procedure to identify such tickets is Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) with rewinding, which requires repeated full trainings and pruning cycles. IMP thus imposes very large computational cost and is practically infeasible to run exhaustively for many different architectures, depths, or large-scale datasets. Alternative one-shot or initialization pruning methods (e.g., SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow, one-shot magnitude) and dynamic sparse training methods reduce some costs but empirically yield subnetworks whose performance and structural properties are often inferior to IMP-found winning tickets. Consequently, there is no established, computationally cheap procedure to obtain high-quality winning tickets for a range of different architectures: researchers must either pay IMP's heavy cost per architecture or accept degraded performance from cheaper methods. This gap prevents amortizing the cost of finding tickets across architectures, blocks theoretical understanding of whether sparse trainable patterns are inherently scalable across architectures, and limits practical adoption of winning-ticket based compressions across model families and deployment targets.

nodes.content: Physical/scientific context: researchers want sparse, trainable subnetworks across multiple architectures of a design family to reduce training/computation cost. Prior state: IMP reliably finds high-quality winning tickets per-architecture but is expensive to run per-target; pruning-at-initialization and dynamic sparse training give cheaper alternatives but produce subnetworks that underperform relative to IMP and exhibit different structural patterns. Consequences of the gap: without a way to derive high-quality tickets for many architectures from a single source, practitioners must run IMP repeatedly (high cost) or accept poorer performance; theorists cannot test whether sparse trainable patterns are architecture-scalable. The E-LTH statement addresses this need by proposing transferability across depths within a family.

Physical/scientific context: to operationalize E-LTH one needs a reproducible mapping from a source ticket (weights and mask) to a target architecture with different depth that preserves sparsity and trainability. Prior approaches for architecture changes (e.g., Net2Net, Network Morphism) preserve function for dense weights but either create dense/identity-initialized layers or break sparse mask structure, making them incompatible with IMP-style sparse tickets. Consequence: without a concrete transformation protocol, the hypothesis is not actionable; ETTs supply explicit choices (unit, invariants, replication/dropping, ordering) so tickets can be transported across depths.

Physical/scientific context: practitioners need to obtain high-quality sparse subnetworks for many target depths without running IMP on each target. Prior state: pruning-at-initialization methods and one-shot magnitude pruning can produce masks for a target but often underperform IMP by clear margins; naively copying masks to extra blocks is insufficient. Consequence: a practical transformation method must produce transferred tickets whose trained accuracy is competitive with target-IMP; the CIFAR-10 experiments test whether ETTs meet that requirement and provide quantitative evidence that they do for ResNet and VGG families at multiple sparsity levels.

Physical/scientific context: large-scale datasets and models (ImageNet, ResNet family) are the practical regimes where IMP is most costly, so any transfer method must be validated at scale. Prior state: many cheap pruning methods fail to match IMP quality on ImageNet; transferring a ticket from a smaller source to a larger target is attractive if it retains high accuracy. Consequence: demonstrating ETTs on ImageNet quantifies whether depth-transferability holds at realistic scale and whether it reduces multiple IMP runs across large targets.

Physical/scientific context: fast pruning-at-initialization methods aim to identify trainable sparse subnetworks without IMP's repeated training; prior empirical studies show they remain inferior to IMP in many cases. Consequence: if ETTs yield better transferred tickets than these initialization pruning methods, practitioners have a cheaper path to high-quality tickets across architectures; the experiments directly compare ETTs vs SNIP/GraSP/one-shot magnitude at matched sparsities to establish this.

Physical/scientific context: dynamic sparse training methods learn sparse networks from scratch per-architecture, reducing per-model cost but still requiring separate runs; a "one-for-all" approach that finds a transferable mask once and reuses it could amortize cost when many targets are required. Prior state: direct cost/accuracy comparisons between DST and any transfer-based approach were lacking. Consequence: the practical utility of E-LTH depends on such comparisons; the reported FLOPs-normalized and accuracy numbers show E-LTH is competitive under realistic accounting and can be more efficient when a mask is reused for multiple target models.

Physical/scientific context: naive replication/dropping of blocks can alter per-stage sparsity distributions, change feature dimensions, or break important estimation steps in residual stages. Prior state: without principled choices, transforming masks may produce poor target tickets. Consequence: the field needs explicit, empirically-validated transformation heuristics to make E-LTH practical; the ablations identify which structural elements must be preserved and which replication strategies work best, especially at high sparsity.

Physical/scientific context: practical deployment often requires changes in both architectural depth and dataset/task; moreover, many architectures include FC layers or mixed layer types. Prior state: it was unclear whether depth-oriented ETTs would break when FC layers are present or when datasets differ. Consequence: demonstrating E-LTH’s applicability beyond convolutional residual stacks is necessary for broader adoption; these preliminary quantitative tests show ETTs can work on FC layers and in cross-dataset scenarios, albeit with measurable drops that need further study.

Physical/scientific context: linear mode connectivity (linear interpolations between independently trained minima) is a property observed for IMP-found winning tickets and indicates basin-preserving optimization behavior; whether transferred tickets occupy similar basins is an open empirical question. Prior state: other sparse masks typically lose connectivity and suffer severe interpolation degradation. Consequence: understanding linear mode connectivity of transferred tickets informs when transfer is likely to succeed (source/target closeness) and suggests that some transfers stay in the same basin while others do not.

Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH): For networks within the same design family (architectures that share stage structure and repeating blocks, e.g., ResNets or VGGs), a winning ticket (a subnetwork characterized by a binary mask and weights rewound to an early training point) found by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on one network (the source) can be transformed into a competitive winning ticket for another network in the same family (the target) of different depth by mindfully replicating (for deeper targets), dropping (for shallower targets), and re-ordering the source network's layers/blocks and their corresponding binary mask, producing a subnetwork for the target that attains performance nearly as high as a winning ticket obtained by running IMP directly on the target.

metadata.narrative: The E-LTH claim relies on the untested generalization to other design families (P1) and the empirically observed failure at large depth gaps (P2). P1 is a generalization weakness: the hypothesis has only been validated on ResNet and VGG families, and its validity for other families (e.g., MobileNets, EfficientNets, Transformers) is entirely unknown. P2 is a scope weakness: even within the ResNet family, large depth gaps (e.g., ResNet-14 to ResNet-44/56) cause ETTs to degrade to baseline level, showing that the claim is not universally true across all depth differences. No highlights are directly assigned to this conclusion, meaning no specific element of the derivation rises above the field's default to underwrite the high-level hypothesis. The practical impact of E-LTH is therefore bounded to the tested families and depth ranges.

nodes.title: Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH) for networks in the same design family

nodes.content: Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) are a concrete set of transformation mappings \(g(\cdot,\cdot)\) and \(h(\cdot,\cdot)\) that take a source winning ticket's rewound weights (weights from an early training stage, i.e., after a small number of training steps) and binary mask (a binary vector indicating retained weights) and construct target-network weights and mask by (a) choosing a minimal replication unit (residual block in ResNets, convolution+normalization layer in VGG), (b) preserving invariant components (number of stages, down-sampling blocks, and input/output layers), (c) replicating selected source units to deepen the network or dropping selected units to shorten it, and (d) choosing replication ordering strategies (appending or interpolation). ETTs keep the source mask structure for existing units and copy masks/weights into replicated units; they aim to approximately preserve per-stage sparsity (fraction of zero weights per stage) while producing target masks usable without running Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on the target.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 describes the methodological construction of Elastic Ticket Transformations; it is a definition rather than an empirical claim and thus carries no load-bearing uncertainties or distinguishing strengths. The construction is internally consistent and follows from the paper's design choices.

nodes.title: Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs): a concrete set of mappings for transferring winning tickets across depths

nodes.content: Applying Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) to transform Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found winning tickets across ResNet and VGG depths on CIFAR-10 yields transferred tickets whose trained accuracies are nearly the same as those of IMP-found winning tickets on the target models across a wide range of sparsities (fraction of zero weights). Representative numerical outcomes: for ResNet-32 at 90% sparsity, the dense model accuracy is 93.83%; E-LTH transferred tickets incur an accuracy drop of -0.96% relative to the dense model (i.e., achieve approximately 92.87%). For ResNet-56 at 90% sparsity, dense accuracy is 94.51% and E-LTH drop is -0.50% (i.e., approximately 94.01%). Across multiple ResNet depths and VGG-13/16/19 transforms, ETTs consistently outperform alternative pruning-at-initialization methods (e.g., SNIP and GraSP), particularly at high sparsities.

metadata.narrative: The CIFAR-10 results (C3) are supported by the Reinit baseline (H3) which isolates the mask contribution from initialization effects, providing causal evidence that the mask itself carries trainability. However, the sparsity alignment uncertainty (P3) could affect the reported quantitative closeness to IMP: if the sparsity ratios are not exactly matched, the small observed gaps (e.g., -0.96% for ResNet-32) might be partially explained by parameter count differences. H3 guards against the initialization confound, but P3 remains an unresolved measurement risk about the fairness of the comparison. The overall evidence is strong, but the quantitative precision is limited by the unreported sparsity matching.

nodes.title: ETT-transferred winning tickets closely match IMP performance on CIFAR-10 across ResNet and VGG models

nodes.content: On ImageNet at sparsity 73.79% (fraction of zero weights), Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets for ResNet architectures attain top-1 accuracies close to Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found tickets and substantially above pruning-at-initialization baselines (e.g., SNIP and GraSP). The reported accuracies are: dense model top-1 accuracies: ResNet-18 69.96%, ResNet-26 72.56%, ResNet-34 73.77%; IMP accuracies: 70.22%, 72.94%, 74.20% respectively; ETTs transferred from ResNet-26 yield ResNet-18: 68.17%, ResNet-34: 73.37%; ETTs transferred from ResNet-18 yield ResNet-26: 71.29%, ResNet-34: 71.86%. Compared to SNIP (e.g., 62.23%, 67.51%, 69.35%) and GraSP (62.85%, 67.24%, 69.23%), ETTs are much closer to IMP.

metadata.narrative: The ImageNet results (C4) benefit from the demonstration at scale (H7), which shows that the depth-transfer mechanism works on large-scale data and substantially outperforms pruning-at-initialization baselines. However, the conclusion is limited by the single sparsity level tested (P4). The paper's own CIFAR-10 results show that ETT-IMP gaps vary with sparsity, and without testing other sparsities on ImageNet, the claim that ETTs "produce competitive transferred tickets on ImageNet at high sparsity" is only weakly supported for sparsities other than 73.79%. H7 underwrites the existence of transfer at scale, but P4 restricts the scope to one sparsity regime.

nodes.title: ETT-transferred tickets approach IMP performance on ImageNet at 73.79% sparsity

nodes.content: Across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet experiments, transferred tickets produced by Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) substantially outperform state-of-the-art pruning-at-initialization methods (e.g., SNIP, GraSP) and one-shot magnitude pruning baselines at matched sparsity levels (fraction of zero weights). Example ImageNet numbers: for ResNet-26 at 73.79% sparsity, SNIP = 67.51%, GraSP = 67.24%, one-shot magnitude pruning = 68.51%, while ETTs transferred from ResNet-18 achieve 71.29% and Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) = 72.94%. On CIFAR-10, similar superior performance gaps are observed across multiple ResNet and VGG depth transforms at sparsities above 80%.

metadata.narrative: The superior performance over pruning-at-initialization baselines (C5) is robustly demonstrated across multiple architectures, datasets, and baselines (H2), providing strong comparative evidence. However, the comparison is confounded by the use of rewound weights for ETTs versus random initialization for baselines (P5). The Reinit baseline (H3, assigned to C3) partially addresses this by showing that the mask alone (with random init) outperforms random pruning, but the full ETT (mask+rewound weights) further outperforms Reinit, meaning the observed margin over SNIP/GraSP is a combination of mask quality and initialization advantage. Thus, the conclusion that ETTs outperform these baselines is well-supported, but the attribution of the advantage to mask superiority (as opposed to better initialization) is less certain due to P5.

nodes.title: ETT-transferred tickets substantially outperform pruning-at-initialization baselines across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet

nodes.content: When comparing total computational cost (FLOPs) and accuracy over a suite of target models, Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH)—where Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) is run once on a source model and Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) produce tickets for multiple targets—achieves comparable accuracies to dynamic sparse training (DST) methods while being cost-competitive or cheaper when amortized across multiple target architectures. Representative comparisons on ImageNet with ResNet-18/26/34 at 73.79% sparsity (using ResNet-26 as source) show E-LTH accuracies: ResNet-18 68.17%, ResNet-26 72.94%, ResNet-34 73.37%, versus RigL (a DST method) with 5x training (RigL-5x) accuracies: 69.59%, 72.66%, 73.88%. FLOPs normalized by the FLOPs of one-pass standard dense training on ResNet-34: RigL requires up to 1.30x normalized FLOPs for ResNet-34, while E-LTH uses 2.77x FLOPs once for source IMP plus small per-target training (0.14x for ResNet-18, 0.20x for ResNet-26, 0.26x for ResNet-34), making E-LTH comparable overall and more favorable as the number of target architectures increases. Against DPF (dynamic model pruning with feedback) on CIFAR-10, E-LTH matches or slightly improves accuracy drops at 90% and 95% sparsity and uses lower total FLOPs (1.26 billion FLOPs vs 1.49 billion FLOPs) to obtain sparse models across five ResNet variants (ResNet-14, -20, -32, -44, -56).

metadata.narrative: The cost-competitiveness claim (C6) is supported by explicit FLOPs accounting (H4), which demonstrates that for the tested configurations (ImageNet at 73.79% sparsity, CIFAR-10 at 90%/95% sparsity), E-LTH's total cost is comparable to or lower than DST methods when amortized over multiple target architectures. However, the cost comparison is sensitive to the number of source IMP iterations (P6), which grows with target sparsity. Higher sparsity regimes would require more IMP iterations on the source, increasing the fixed cost and potentially eroding the advantage. H4 provides a concrete baseline, but P6 introduces uncertainty about the conclusion's validity at higher sparsities or for different numbers of target architectures.

nodes.title: E-LTH achieves comparable accuracy to dynamic sparse training at competitive amortized computational cost

nodes.content: Empirical ablations on CIFAR-10 using ResNet-32 and ResNet-56 yield actionable design rules for Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) when transferring winning tickets across ResNet depths: (a) choose minimal replication units consistent with model structure (residual blocks for ResNets; convolutional layer plus normalization layer for VGG); (b) preserve number of stages (groups of blocks delimited by down-sampling), down-sampling blocks, and input/output layers; (c) when stretching (deepening), prefer replicating more distinct source blocks fewer times (i.e., replicate unique units) rather than repeating the same unit many times to better preserve per-stage sparsity (fraction of zero weights per stage); (d) replication ordering can be interpolation (replicated block inserted immediately after its source block) or appending (replicated blocks appended after the last block) with comparable performance; (e) prefer replicating or dropping later blocks less aggressively and avoid dropping too many early blocks (dropping many early blocks degrades accuracy); (f) these choices matter more at high sparsity levels.

metadata.narrative: The ablation-derived rules (C7) are empirically grounded by systematic comparisons (H1) that isolate the effect of each design choice (number of replicated blocks, ordering, dropping position) across multiple sparsity levels. H1 shows that the rules are not arbitrary: violating them (e.g., replicating fewer unique blocks, dropping many early blocks) leads to measurable accuracy degradation. However, the rules are validated only for the ResNet-32→56 transfer on CIFAR-10 (P7), and their applicability to other design families or larger depth gaps is untested. The credit from H1 is strong within the tested regime, but P7 limits the generalization of the rules beyond that regime.

nodes.title: Ablation-derived design rules for effective ETT construction on ResNets

nodes.content: Preliminary experiments show Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) can transfer winning tickets that include fully-connected (FC) layers and can be combined with dataset transfer. (a) For VGG variants with differing numbers of FC layers (VGG-13-2, VGG-13-3, VGG-13-5) and for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) of varying widths on MNIST, E-LTH (the Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis approach) transfers at 89.26% sparsity (fraction of zero weights) with ≤0.21% accuracy differences relative to directly trained winning tickets. (b) Transferring tickets across datasets and architectures shows that dataset shifts cause an accuracy drop and architectural shifts cause another drop, but these drops do not simply add linearly. For example, transferring a ResNet-20 winning ticket from SVHN to CIFAR-10 and from ResNet-20 to ResNet-32 simultaneously yields a 3.55% net accuracy drop compared to the Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) baseline on the target (ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10: IMP accuracy 92.22% versus transferred accuracy 88.67%), demonstrating partial robustness. (c) For ImageNet to CIFAR-10 transfer, ETTs from ResNet-18 to ResNet-18 achieve 95.40% top-1 accuracy (dense model: 95.21%, IMP: 95.42%), and ETTs from ResNet-18 to ResNet-26 achieve 95.16%, showing small drops.

metadata.narrative: The generalization to FC layers and cross-dataset shifts (C8) is supported by the non-additive interaction finding (H6), which suggests that architecture and dataset shifts do not compound linearly, a favorable property for combined transfer. However, the underlying evidence is very limited in scope (two dataset pairs, one architecture pair, simple MLP on MNIST) (P8). The paper correctly describes these as preliminary tests, so the conclusion's strength is appropriately weak. H6 provides the main empirical highlight, but P8 shows that the scope of validation is too narrow to support a confident claim of generalization.

nodes.title: E-LTH generalizes to fully-connected layers and shows partial robustness across dataset shifts in preliminary tests

nodes.content: Transferred tickets via Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) can exhibit linear mode connectivity (the property that a linear interpolation of the parameters of two independently trained models achieves test accuracy comparable to the endpoints) similar to Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found winning tickets when the source and target are close in depth, but connectivity stability degrades as depth difference increases. Quantitatively: ETTs transferred from ResNet-20 to ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity show a maximum interpolation accuracy drop of 8.72%, whereas ETTs from ResNet-14 to ResNet-32 show a much larger maximal drop of 69.72%. IMP-found tickets remain stable under linear interpolation (maximal drop near zero). Thus, ETTs better preserve linear connectivity when source and target belong to the same loss basin (smaller depth gap).

metadata.narrative: The linear mode connectivity claim (C9) relies on a single successful case (ResNet-20→32 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity) with a moderate 8.72% maximum accuracy drop, and is contradicted by the severe failure case (ResNet-14→32, 69.72% drop) (P9). H5 provides a mechanistic insight by quantifying connectivity and linking it to depth gap, but the extremely narrow evidence base (one target architecture, two sources) means that the conclusion that "ETTs can exhibit linear mode connectivity" is only supported for a very specific regime and is not a general property. The failure case directly undermines any broad claim. P9 shows that the conclusion is very weakly supported overall.

nodes.title: Linear mode connectivity of ETT-transferred tickets degrades with larger depth gaps

nodes.content: The Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH)—that a winning ticket (a sparse subnetwork characterized by a binary mask and weights rewound to an early training point, found by Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)) from a source network can be transformed via Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) into a competitive ticket for a target network of different depth within the same design family—has been experimentally validated only on the ResNet family (on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet) and the VGG family (on CIFAR-10). No experiments are reported for other design families that share the defining structural properties of repeating blocks and stage structure, such as MobileNets, EfficientNets, or Transformers.

metadata.failure_mode: If E-LTH fails for another design family (e.g., EfficientNet), the conclusion that E-LTH holds for "networks within the same design family" would be false for that family, confining the hypothesis to only ResNets and VGGs. The practical claim that one IMP run can be amortized across many architectures would then not apply to families outside those tested, significantly limiting the method's generality.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper acknowledges that many models are designed in families (MobileNets, EfficientNets, Transformers) and suggests E-LTH may apply, but provides no experimental evidence. The structural properties of these families differ from ResNet/VGG (e.g., inverted residuals, attention mechanisms, depthwise separable convolutions), and transferability may depend on architectural features beyond block repetition. Without such evidence, the claim that E-LTH holds for any network in the same design family overreaches the data.

nodes.title: E-LTH experimentally validated only on ResNet and VGG families

nodes.content: For the ResNet family on CIFAR-10, when the source network is much shallower than the target (e.g., ResNet-14 transferred to ResNet-44 or ResNet-56), the test accuracy of the Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets at sparsity levels above 80% (fraction of zero weights) degrades to a level that is no better than the pruning-at-initialization baselines SNIP and GraSP. In contrast, transfers between closer depths (e.g., ResNet-32 to ResNet-56) maintain a clear margin over these baselines across the full sparsity range.Figure 6

metadata.failure_mode: If the weak point is true (i.e., large depth gaps cause failure), then the conclusion that ETTs produce competitive tickets for any target depth within the family is false for the regime where depth difference exceeds a moderate threshold. For very deep targets, one would still need to run IMP on the source or find a closer source, undermining the "once-for-all" benefit.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's own results (Figure 6) show that the gap between ETTs and pruning-at-initialization baselines vanishes for large depth gaps. The authors explicitly note that "replicating or dropping strategies potentially still introduce noise, which may be acceptable within a moderate range, but might become too amplified when replicating or dropping too many times." The conclusion's claim that ETTs work for any target depth difference is thus empirically bounded, and the bound is not quantified.

nodes.title: Large depth gap causes ETT accuracy to degrade to baseline level on CIFAR-10 ResNets

nodes.content: In the CIFAR-10 experiments evaluating Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets against Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP)-found tickets, the sparsity ratios (fraction of zero weights) of the compared subnetworks may not be exactly matched because replicating and dropping blocks during ETTs changes the total number of parameters and the resulting sparsity ratio in a less controllable way. The paper acknowledges this and states that "all pruning methods will match the sparsity ratios of the winning tickets generated by IMP, to the best possible extent." The actual sparsity ratios achieved for ETTs and for the other pruning methods are not reported, so the degree of mismatch and its potential impact on accuracy comparisons is unknown.

metadata.failure_mode: If ETT masks have, for example, 89.5% sparsity when IMP masks have 90%, the extra 0.5% parameters could inflate ETT accuracy by a non-negligible amount, potentially making the gap to IMP appear smaller than it really is. The conclusion that ETT tickets nearly match IMP tickets could then be an artifact of slightly unequal sparsity, weakening its support.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not present the exact sparsity ratios achieved for each method. If ETTs systematically produce slightly lower sparsity (retaining more parameters) than IMP, their accuracy advantage could be partially attributed to higher parameter count rather than superior mask structure. Conversely, if ETTs are sparser, they could be at an unfair disadvantage. Without these numbers, the quantitative comparisons lack the precision needed to confirm that the observed accuracies are due to mask quality alone, especially when the reported gaps to IMP are small (below 1%).

nodes.title: Potential sparsity mismatch between ETT and IMP tickets due to block replication/dropping

nodes.content: The ImageNet experiments for Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets are conducted at a single sparsity level of 73.79% (fraction of zero weights), which is the level at which Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) with rewinding successfully identifies winning tickets (as reported in prior work). No experiments are reported at other sparsity levels (e.g., 80%, 90%) for ImageNet models. Therefore, the claim that ETTs produce competitive transferred tickets on ImageNet at high sparsity is supported only at this one specific sparsity.Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If at higher sparsities on ImageNet (e.g., 90% sparsity) the ETT accuracies degrade faster than IMP accuracies, the conclusion that ETTs "produce competitive transferred tickets on ImageNet at high sparsity" would not hold at those sparsities. The valid regime of the claim would be narrower than stated.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's own CIFAR-10 results (Figure 1) show that the relative performance of ETTs versus other methods can vary with sparsity; at some sparsities, the gap to IMP is larger. On ImageNet, the behavior at other sparsities is unknown because experiments were not performed. Choosing the sparsity where IMP is known to work could be a favorable setting for ETTs; at higher sparsities, the transfer may degrade as seen on CIFAR-10.

nodes.title: ImageNet evaluation at only one sparsity level (73.79%)

nodes.content: In the comparison of Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) with pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP, one-shot magnitude pruning), ETTs use the rewound weights (weights after training for 1,000 steps on CIFAR-10 or 5 epochs on ImageNet) from the source Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) run as the starting point for training on the target network. SNIP, GraSP, and one-shot magnitude pruning use randomly initialized weights. Although the paper includes a "Reinit" baseline where the ETT mask is used with reinitialized weights, this baseline does not control for the possibility that the rewound weights provide a better starting point that boosts final accuracy beyond what the mask alone would achieve starting from random initialization.

metadata.failure_mode: If the rewound weights are the dominant factor in the accuracy advantage, then the conclusion that ETT masks are superior to SNIP/GraSP masks is only partially supported; the observed gap could be largely due to better initialization rather than better mask structure. This would weaken the claim that the mask transformation is the primary reason for outperformance.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's Reinit baseline shows that the mask alone (with random init) outperforms SNIP/GraSP, which supports the mask quality claim. However, the full ETT (mask + rewound weights) further outperforms Reinit, showing that the rewound weights contribute additional benefit. Therefore, the observed advantage of ETTs over SNIP/GraSP is a combination of mask quality and initialization quality, not just mask superiority. A strict comparison of mask quality would require controlling initialization.

nodes.title: Initialization confound in ETT vs. pruning-at-initialization comparison

nodes.content: In the cost comparison with RigL (a dynamic sparse training method) on ImageNet, Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH) runs 7 iterations of Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP) on the source ResNet-26 to reach 73.79% sparsity. The total normalized FLOPs (relative to the FLOPs of one-pass standard dense training on ResNet-34) for E-LTH (3.37x) is similar to RigL's (2.99x). The number of IMP iterations required to reach a given sparsity grows logarithmically with the inverse of sparsity; for higher sparsity targets (e.g., 90%), more iterations would be needed. The paper does not explore how the cost comparison changes for higher sparsities or for different numbers of target architectures beyond the three tested (ResNet-18, -26, -34).Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If, to reach 90% sparsity on ImageNet, 15 IMP iterations are needed (2x cost), the E-LTH total FLOPs would become 7.77x for the three targets, making it substantially more expensive than RigL's 2.99x. The conclusion that E-LTH is competitive with DST under amortized cost would then be false for higher sparsity regimes.
metadata.weakness_reason: The cost advantage of E-LTH relies on the source IMP cost (fixed) being amortized over multiple target architectures. If higher sparsity requires more source iterations, the fixed cost increases, making the amortization less favorable, especially for small numbers of targets. The paper does not provide sensitivity analysis on the number of IMP iterations or the number of target architectures, so the claim that E-LTH is "cost-competitive" is tied to the specific experimental configuration.

nodes.title: Cost comparison with RigL depends on sparsity target and number of architectures

nodes.content: The design rules for Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs) derived from ablations (replicate more unique blocks rather than few blocks many times, preserve early blocks during squeezing, use either interpolation or appending ordering) are based on experiments on the ResNet family, specifically transferring between ResNet-32 and ResNet-56 on CIFAR-10, with additional supporting results for VGG. The rules have not been validated for other design families (e.g., MobileNets, EfficientNets) or for depth gaps larger than the ones tested within ResNets.Figures 4, 5

metadata.failure_mode: If the ablation-derived rules fail to produce good tickets in another design family (e.g., MobileNet), then the conclusion that these rules are effective guidelines for ETT construction would be false for that family, limiting their general utility.
metadata.weakness_reason: The ablation experiments cover a limited subset of possible transformations. The rules rely on properties of ResNet-style residual blocks (e.g., skip connections) that may not hold in other families (e.g., inverted residuals with linear bottlenecks). The paper acknowledges that width transformations are much harder, suggesting that the rules are not universally applicable. Without validation in other families, the rules remain heuristics specific to the tested architectures.

nodes.title: ETT design rules derived from limited ResNet and VGG ablations on CIFAR-10

nodes.content: The cross-dataset transfer experiments combine architecture transfer (ResNet-20 to ResNet-32) and dataset transfer (SVHN to CIFAR-10, ImageNet to CIFAR-10). The results show accuracy drops of 3.55% for SVHN to CIFAR-10 with architecture transfer (ResNet-20 to ResNet-32), and a nearly zero drop for ImageNet to CIFAR-10 with architecture transfer (using upsampled CIFAR-10 images). The experiments are limited to two dataset pairs and one architecture transfer pair. The paper calls these "preliminary tests."Tables 6, 7

metadata.failure_mode: If cross-dataset transfer works only for specific combinations (e.g., datasets with similar distribution or architectures with close depth), the conclusion that E-LTH generalizes across dataset shifts would be false for the many other scenarios where a practitioner might want to apply it.
metadata.weakness_reason: The evidence is very limited: only two dataset shifts (SVHN/CIFAR-10, ImageNet/CIFAR-10) and one architecture pair are tested. The non-negligible drop (3.55%) in the SVHN→CIFAR-10 case shows that transfer is not lossless. The ImageNet→CIFAR-10 case uses image upsampling to match input size, which is a nontrivial preprocessing change. Without testing on more diverse dataset pairs (e.g., CIFAR-100 to ImageNet) or architecture pairs, the generality of cross-dataset transfer is unestablished.

nodes.title: Cross-dataset generalization tested only on two dataset pairs and one architecture pair

nodes.content: The linear mode connectivity (the property that linear interpolation of two independently trained models' parameters yields comparable accuracy) property of Elastic Ticket Transformation (ETT)-transferred tickets is tested on a single target model (ResNet-32 on CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity) with two source models: ResNet-20 (producing a maximum accuracy drop of 8.72% along linear interpolation) and ResNet-14 (producing a maximum drop of 69.72%). No experiments are performed on other architectures (e.g., VGG, deeper ResNets), other datasets (e.g., ImageNet), or other sparsity levels.Figure 8

metadata.failure_mode: If the claim is that ETTs can exhibit linear mode connectivity, the weak point shows that this is only true for a very narrow regime (source and target close in depth, specific architecture, specific dataset). The failure case (ResNet-14→32) shows that connectivity cannot be assumed, so the conclusion's scope is extremely limited.
metadata.weakness_reason: The connectivity experiment is extremely limited in scope. The successful case (ResNet-20→32) shows a moderate drop of 8.72%, which is not as stable as the near-zero drop of IMP tickets, and the failure case (ResNet-14→32) shows catastrophic degradation. The paper's conclusion that "ETTs can exhibit linear mode connectivity" relies entirely on the moderate-success case; the failure case directly contradicts the idea that connectivity is a general property of ETTs. Without broader evidence, the claim is not robust.

nodes.title: Linear mode connectivity tested only on one target model and two source models on CIFAR-10

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10, for the transformation from ResNet-32 to ResNet-56 via ETTs, the systematic ablation reported in Figures 4 and 5 compares replicating four unique blocks, two unique blocks, or one block repeated, for both appending and interpolation ordering, across multiple sparsity levels (50%–96%). The results show that replicating all four unique blocks consistently yields higher test accuracy than replicating fewer, with larger gaps at higher sparsities. The ordering choice (interpolation vs appending) produces comparable performance. During squeezing (ResNet-56 to ResNet-32), dropping early blocks (the first four of five) causes severe degradation, while dropping later blocks or a mix of early and late blocks is safe. All trends are averaged over three independent runs with error bars shown.

metadata.credit: This ablation provides the empirical basis for each design rule in conclusion 7. Without it, the design choices would be untested assumptions. The direct comparison of options (e.g., 4 vs 2 vs 1 blocks) guards against the failure mode that any replication strategy works equally well, showing that the choice matters and that the identified rules (prefer more unique blocks, preserve early blocks) are load-bearing. The error bars and multi-sparsity coverage ensure the trends are not artifacts of a single configuration.

nodes.title: Systematic ablation of design choices

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10, across five ResNet depths (ResNet-14, 20, 32, 44, 56) and three VGG depths (VGG-13, 16, 19), and on ImageNet across three ResNet depths (ResNet-18, 26, 34) at 73.79% sparsity, ETT-transferred tickets achieve test accuracies that are consistently higher than those from SNIP, GraSP, and one-shot magnitude pruning at matched sparsity levels. Representative margins: on ImageNet ResNet-34, ETTs (←26) achieve 73.37% vs SNIP 69.35% (4.0% gap); on CIFAR-10 ResNet-56 at 90% sparsity, ETTs (from ResNet-32) achieve ~94.01% vs SNIP ~88% (~6% gap). The advantage persists at low, medium, and high sparsities.

metadata.credit: This highlight provides the core empirical validation for conclusion 5. The breadth of the comparison (two families, two datasets, three baselines, multiple sparsities) guards against the failure that the advantage is specific to a particular architecture or dataset. The consistent large margins show that the outperformance is a robust property of ETTs, not a statistical fluctuation.

nodes.title: Consistent outperformance over SNIP/GraSP across families and datasets

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-32 as source and ResNet-56 as target (Figure 3), the "Reinit" baseline, which applies the ETT mask but reinitializes the weights (random init), yields significantly lower test accuracy than the full ETT (mask + source rewound weights) at sparsity levels above 50%. The "Random" baseline (random mask with random weights) performs even worse. This shows that the mask structure alone, without the benefit of rewound weights, still substantially outperforms random pruning and provides a large part of the transfer success.

metadata.credit: This baseline directly controls for the confound that ETTs might succeed solely due to better initialization from rewound weights. The Reinit result shows that the mask carries significant trainability information beyond the starting weights. Without this control, the conclusion that ETTs produce high-quality masks (conclusion 3) would be vulnerable to the alternative explanation that any mask with rewound weights works well. The credit specifically underwrites the attribution of success to the mask structure.

nodes.title: Reinit baseline isolates mask contribution

nodes.content: For producing sparse ResNet-18/26/34 models on ImageNet at 73.79% sparsity, the total normalized FLOPs (relative to one dense ResNet-34 training) for E-LTH (source IMP on ResNet-26: 2.77x, plus per-target training: 0.14x+0.20x+0.26x) is 3.37x. RigL-5x totals 0.69x+1.0x+1.30x = 2.99x. For five CIFAR-10 ResNet variants at 90% and 95% sparsity, E-LTH uses 1.26 billion FLOPs while DPF uses 1.49 billion FLOPs. The paper reports that E-LTH accuracy is competitive (e.g., ImageNet ResNet-34: 73.37% vs RigL 73.88%; CIFAR-10 ResNet-32 at 90%: -0.96% vs DPF -1.41%).

metadata.credit: This highlight grounds conclusion 6 in explicit FLOPs numbers, guarding against the failure mode that the cost advantage is merely claimed without quantification. The comparison shows that for the tested settings, E-LTH is within a small factor of DST cost and can be cheaper when more targets are added. Without this, the conclusion would be speculative. The credit underwrites the quantitative cost-competitiveness claim.

nodes.title: Explicit FLOPs comparison with RigL and DPF

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 at 90% sparsity, linear interpolation between two independently trained ETT-transferred tickets from ResNet-20 to ResNet-32 yields a maximum accuracy drop of 8.72% along the interpolation path from the endpoint accuracies. For tickets transferred from ResNet-14 to ResNet-32, the maximum drop is 69.72%. IMP-found tickets on ResNet-32 show a near-zero drop. The result is shown in Figure 8 for a single configuration.

metadata.credit: This highlight provides the first evidence that ETT tickets from close depth transfers approximately stay in the same loss basin as IMP tickets. The connectivity measure guards against the failure that transferred tickets occupy entirely different basins and thus cannot be stably optimized. The near-zero drop for IMP and moderate drop for ResNet-20→32 (compared to severe drop for ResNet-14→32) supports the claim in conclusion 9 that connectivity is maintained when source and target are close in depth, and also provides a mechanistic explanation for the depth-gap limitation.

nodes.title: Linear mode connectivity measurement for close-depth transfer

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 and SVHN, the combined transfer (architecture: ResNet-20 to ResNet-32, dataset: SVHN to CIFAR-10) yields a net accuracy drop of 3.55% relative to the IMP baseline (92.22%). The individual drops are 0.32% (architecture only) and 3.86% (dataset only). The combined drop is less than the sum and slightly less than the dataset-only drop, indicating non-additive interaction. The experiment uses a single architecture pair and two datasets.

metadata.credit: This highlight supports conclusion 8 by demonstrating that the two transfer dimensions do not compound additively, which is a favorable property for practical combined transfer. Without this experiment, one might pessimistically assume that drops add, making combined transfer impractical. The non-additivity result suggests some robustness, lending credibility to the claim that E-LTH works across dataset shifts.

nodes.title: Non-additive degradation in cross-dataset+architecture transfer

nodes.content: On ImageNet at 73.79% sparsity, ETTs produce transferred tickets from ResNet-26 to ResNet-34 achieving 73.37% top-1 accuracy, compared to IMP's 74.20% (gap 0.83%) and SNIP's 69.35% (gap 4.02%). From ResNet-18 to ResNet-34, ETTs achieve 71.86%, still 1.14% above SNIP. The experiments use the standard ImageNet training schedule (Table 4) with three ResNet architectures.

metadata.credit: This highlight directly shows that the depth-transfer mechanism scales to large-scale datasets, which is necessary for practical relevance. Without these ImageNet results, the conclusion that ETTs produce competitive tickets on ImageNet would be unsupported; the CIFAR-10 results could be dismissed as not representative of large-scale behavior. The credit underwrites the scope of conclusion 4: the method is not limited to small-scale experiments.

nodes.title: Scaled validation on ImageNet

steps.reasoning: Treat as known the empirical fact that ETTs (conclusion 2) provide a concrete method to transform a source IMP-found ticket's rewound weights and binary mask into target-network weights and mask by selecting a minimal replication unit, preserving invariants (stages, down-sampling blocks, input/output), replicating or dropping units, copying masks/weights into replicated units, and choosing replication ordering strategies; also treat as known that ETTs produce high-quality transferred tickets in CIFAR-10 experiments (conclusion 3) and competitive results on ImageNet (conclusion 4).

Provide the formal statement of Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH) using the paper's notation: given a source network winning ticket represented by rewound weights $\\theta_r^{s}$ and binary mask $m^{s}$ (i.e., the sparse subnetwork $f^{s}(\\theta_r^{s} \\odot m^{s})$ found by IMP), there exist transformation mappings $g(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ and $h(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ (the ETTs) such that the constructed target subnetwork $f^{t}\\bigl(g(\\theta_r^{s},m^{s}),\\; h(\\theta_r^{s},m^{s})\\bigr)$ for another network $f^{t}$ in the same design family but of different depth attains performance nearly as high as a winning ticket obtained by running IMP directly on $f^{t}$. This is the hypothesis statement articulated in the paper.

Explain the restrictions and scope embedded in E-LTH: the hypothesis is asserted for networks within the same design family (i.e., architectures that share stage structure and repeating blocks such as ResNets or VGGs) and the transformations considered are depth changes (stretching to deeper networks via replication, or squeezing to shallower networks via dropping), while preserving stage-level invariants so that dimensions remain compatible; these modeling constraints are explicitly stated in the paper as part of the hypothesis scope.
Fig2

Summarize empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis drawn from the paper: (a) CIFAR-10 experiments across ResNet and VGG families show ETT-transferred tickets reach accuracies nearly matching IMP targets across many sparsities (conclusion 3; Figures 1,3,6,7, Table 3); (b) ImageNet experiments on ResNet-18/26/34 at 73.79% sparsity show ETTs attain accuracies close to IMP and far above SNIP/GraSP baselines (conclusion 4; Table 1). These empirical results are cited in the hypothesis statement as support for its claim that transferred tickets can be competitive.
Fig1
Fig6

State the procedural content of the hypothesis that makes it operational: E-LTH is not merely an existence statement but is accompanied by the ETT operational protocol ($g,h$) that prescribes how to replicate/drop/re-order minimal units and how to copy masks/weights into replicated units so that the transformed mask is directly usable for training the target without re-running full IMP on the target; this operationalization is what makes E-LTH actionable in practice.
Fig2

Clarify the intended consequence emphasized by the paper: if E-LTH holds under these same-family depth transformations, then a single IMP run on a source architecture can be amortized to produce high-quality tickets across multiple target depths within the family, saving computational cost and enabling exploration of whether sparse trainable patterns are scalable across architectures; the paper uses the empirical results to claim this practical and theoretical implication.

Define notation for a winning ticket on a source network: let $f^{s}$ denote the source network, let $\\theta_r^{s}$ denote the rewound weights after $r$ training steps (where $r$ is the rewinding step count used in Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning with rewinding), and let $m^{s}$ denote the binary mask of the source winning ticket, where the mask $m^{s}$ has the same shape as $\\theta_r^{s}$ and $\\odot$ denotes element-wise (Hadamard) product; thus the source winning ticket is the sparse subnetwork $f^{s}(\\theta_r^{s} \\odot m^{s})$ as stated in the paper.
[13]

State the objective of Elastic Ticket Transformations (ETTs): construct two mapping functions $g(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ and $h(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ that take the source rewound weights $\\theta_r^{s}$ and source mask $m^{s}$ as inputs and produce target-network rewound weights and target mask, i.e., construct a target ticket $f^{t}\\bigl(g(\\theta_r^{s},m^{s}),\\; h(\\theta_r^{s},m^{s})\\bigr)$ for a target architecture $f^{t}$ that differs in depth from the source, thereby avoiding re-running expensive IMP on the target.

Specify the minimal replication unit choices used by ETTs (the first concrete design decision): (a) for networks built from repeated convolutional layers (e.g., VGG family), treat a convolution (or linear) layer together with its associated normalization layer as the minimal unit for replication/drop; (b) for residual-style networks (e.g., ResNets), treat the entire residual block (including its convolutional layers, normalization layers, and shortcut) as the minimal replication unit, motivated by residual blocks being the natural repeating unit and by dynamical-systems / unrolled-estimation interpretations of residual blocks as a time-step or iterative refinement step.
Fig2
[22]

List invariant components that ETTs preserve when transforming architectures: (a) preserve the number of stages delimited by down-sampling blocks to avoid changing intermediate feature dimensions; (b) transplant down-sampling blocks one-to-one without replicating or dropping them; (c) preserve input and output layers because their dimensions remain consistent when the number of stages is kept constant. These invariances constrain $g$ and $h$ to only replicate/drop within-stage units while keeping stage boundaries fixed.

Explain replication vs dropping mechanics in $g$ and $h$: to stretch (deepen) the network, ETTs select certain minimal units and (i) copy the source unit's rewound weights into newly created units in the target and (ii) copy the corresponding mask entries from the source unit into the replicated unit; to squeeze (shallow) the network, ETTs drop selected units and their mask/weight entries. Thus $g(\\theta_r^{s},m^{s})$ copies and places weight tensors for replicated units and passes through weights for preserved units, and $h(\\theta_r^{s},m^{s})$ copies and slices the mask $m^{s}$ to produce the target mask while attempting to preserve per-stage sparsity proportions.

Describe concrete ordering strategies implemented in ETTs (how replicated units are arranged): (a) appending: append replicated copies of selected units after the last occurrence of those units in the stage (i.e., add copies grouped after originals); (b) interpolation: insert each replicated copy immediately after its source unit, effectively interleaving originals and copies. Both ordering schemes are implemented by $g$ and $h$ and were empirically compared.
Fig2

Explain the per-stage sparsity preservation goal and the practical replication choice: ETTs favor replicating a larger set of distinct source units fewer times each (replicate "unique" units) rather than repeating a single source unit many times, because this strategy better preserves stage-wise sparsity ratios (if different source blocks have differing sparsity, proportional replication keeps the overall sparsity near the source) and aligns with a uniform interpolation rationale from the dynamical-systems view.

Contrast ETTs with prior network-transformation works and explain incompatibilities: Net2Net and Network Morphism provide dense-preserving transforms (e.g., identity-like initializations for new layers or layer decompositions) but either introduce dense/identity-initialized layers or break sparse mask structure, making them incompatible with the requirement to transfer an IMP-style sparse mask intact; ETTs instead explicitly copy sparse mask entries into replicated units so that the target mask remains a sparse IMP-style mask usable without re-running IMP on the target.
[4]
[41]

Summarize operational definition of ETTs as the implemented mapping family: ETTs are the set of transformation choices implemented for $g(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ and $h(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ consisting of (i) choice of minimal unit (residual block or layer+norm), (ii) invariants to preserve (stages, down-sampling blocks, input/output), (iii) replication or dropping strategies (which units and how many times), (iv) replication ordering (appending vs interpolation), and (v) mask/weight copying rules (copy masks and rewound weights into replicated units). These mappings produce target weights and mask intended to be directly trainable on the target without performing IMP on the target.
Fig2

Start from the previously established ETTs mapping functions $g(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ and $h(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ that produce target rewound weights and masks by replicating/dropping/re-ordering minimal units and copying masks/weights into replicated units; treat these ETT transformations as given and available to apply to source IMP-found tickets.
Fig2

Experimental setup for CIFAR-10 evaluations: use IMP with rewinding to obtain source winning tickets (rewound weights and masks) on various ResNet and VGG source depths; apply ETT mappings to create target-network masks and weights for different target depths; train the transformed target tickets from the rewound weights under the transferred mask following the paper's training hyperparameters (e.g., 160 epochs, SGD, learning-rate schedule as in the experimental settings) and compare final test accuracies against (a) IMP-found winning tickets trained on each target individually, (b) pruning-at-initialization baselines (SNIP, GraSP), (c) one-shot magnitude, and (d) other ablation baselines (Reinit, Random mask/shuffle). Results are averaged over three independent runs.
[27]

Report that across a wide range of sparsities on CIFAR-10, ETT-transformed tickets trained on the target reach accuracies nearly matching IMP-found winning tickets on those same targets: the paper shows curves (for ResNet and VGG family transfers) where the ETT-transferred ticket accuracy curves lie close to the IMP curves and substantially above SNIP/GraSP/one-shot magnitude baselines, with especially pronounced improvements at high sparsities (>80%). Provide the empirical references: Figures 1, 3, 6, and 7 display these accuracy-vs-sparsity comparisons for ResNets and VGGs.
Fig1
Fig6

Cite representative numerical outcomes from CIFAR-10 ResNet experiments (numerics reproduced from the paper): for ResNet-32 at 90% sparsity the dense model accuracy is reported as $93.83\\%$, and the E-LTH transferred ticket exhibits an accuracy drop of $-0.96\\%$ relative to the dense baseline (i.e., achieves approximately $92.87\\%$); for ResNet-56 at 90% sparsity the dense accuracy is $94.51\\%$ and E-LTH transferred ticket drop is $-0.50\\%$ (i.e., approximately $94.01\\%$). These numbers are reported in the CIFAR-10 comparisons (Table 3 in the paper) and demonstrate ETTs' competitive performance across multiple depths and sparsity levels.
Fig3
Fig7
Fig6
[28]

Provide empirical comparison claim: across multiple ResNet depths and VGG-13/16/19 transfers, ETTs consistently outperform alternative pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP, one-shot magnitude) at matched sparsities, and their accuracy is closely aligned with target-IMP results — especially evident at high sparsities where other initialization pruning methods suffer larger degradations.
Fig1
Fig3

Start from ETTs (the $g,h$ mappings) as implemented (previously established) and apply them in the large-scale experimental regime: instantiate IMP on ImageNet-scale source models (ResNet-18, ResNet-26, ResNet-34) to obtain source winning tickets at a chosen sparsity, then apply ETTs to transform source tickets to target depths and train the resulting target tickets on ImageNet under the transferred masks and rewound weights.
Fig2

Specify ImageNet experimental choices: choose sparsity ratio $73.79\\%$ as the test level where IMP with rewinding is known to successfully identify winning tickets; use the experimental training hyperparameters described in the paper (ImageNet training schedule, rewinding at 5 epochs for ImageNet, etc.); compare ETT-transferred tickets against IMP-found target tickets and against pruning-at-initialization baselines (SNIP, GraSP, one-shot magnitude) and simple baselines (Reinit, Random) as in the CIFAR-10 experiments.
[15]

Report the ImageNet numerical outcomes (reproduced from the paper's Table 1): the dense top-1 accuracies are ResNet-18 $69.96\\%$, ResNet-26 $72.56\\%$, ResNet-34 $73.77\\%$; the IMP top-1 accuracies are $70.22\\%$, $72.94\\%$, $74.20\\%$ respectively. ETT-transferred tickets (examples reported in the paper) include: using ResNet-26 as source to produce ResNet-18 yields $68.17\\%$ and to ResNet-34 yields $73.37\\%$; using ResNet-18 as source to produce ResNet-26 yields $71.29\\%$ and to ResNet-34 yields $71.86\\%$; using ResNet-34 as source provides other transfer numbers shown in the table. These ETT numbers are close to IMP and substantially higher than SNIP/GraSP/one-shot magnitude baselines (e.g., SNIP: $62.23\\%$, $67.51\\%$, $69.35\\%$).
Table1

Conclude that at ImageNet scale and at the tested sparsity $73.79\\%$, ETT-transferred tickets attain accuracies close to IMP-found tickets and are substantially above pruning-at-initialization baselines, thus demonstrating ETTs' effectiveness at realistic scale where IMP cost is high and transfer would be most useful.

Start from ETTs (conclusion 2) and the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet empirical results (conclusions 3 and 4) as established inputs: ETTs are applied to produce transferred tickets and experiments compare those to pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP), one-shot magnitude, and standard baselines (Reinit, Random).

Present ImageNet comparative numbers showing ETT superiority over pruning-at-initialization at matched sparsity (reproduced from Table 1): for ResNet-26 at $73.79\\%$ sparsity, SNIP achieves $67.51\\%$, GraSP $67.24\\%$, one-shot Magnitude $68.51\\%$, while ETTs transferred from ResNet-18 achieve $71.29\\%$ and IMP achieves $72.94\\%$. These numbers show ETTs closer to IMP and substantially above SNIP/GraSP/Magnitude.
Table1

Summarize CIFAR-10 comparative evidence: across multiple CIFAR-10 experiments (Figures 1, 3, 6, 7) ETTs consistently outperform pruning-at-initialization methods (SNIP, GraSP, one-shot magnitude) at matched sparsities, with the advantage being especially large at high sparsities (>80%); refer to plotted accuracy-vs-sparsity curves where ETT curves lie substantially above SNIP/GraSP curves and close to IMP curves.
Fig1
Fig3

Conclude that across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet experiments, transferred tickets produced by ETTs substantially outperform state-of-the-art pruning-at-initialization methods and one-shot magnitude baselines at matched sparsity levels, providing empirical support that ETTs (and thus E-LTH operationalized by ETTs) yields higher-quality transferred tickets than these initialization pruning alternatives.

Treat ETTs and the ability to produce multiple transferred tickets from one source IMP run (E-LTH operationalized) as established; set up the cost-accuracy comparison objective against dynamic sparse training (DST) methods by comparing normalized FLOPs (where FLOPs are normalized to the FLOPs of one-pass dense training on ResNet-34) and final accuracies across a suite of target models, following the paper's FLOPs-normalization protocol.
Table2

Present ImageNet RigL comparison data reproduced from the paper (Table 2): using ResNet-26 as the source, E-LTH yields accuracies ResNet-18 $68.17\\%$, ResNet-26 $72.94\\%$, ResNet-34 $73.37\\%$; RigL-5x yields $69.59\\%$, $72.66\\%$, $73.88\\%$ respectively. For FLOPs, RigL uses normalized FLOPs $0.69x$ for ResNet-18, $1.0x$ for ResNet-26, and $1.30x$ for ResNet-34 (due to 5x training for RigL); E-LTH first expends $2.77x$ FLOPs to run IMP once on ResNet-26, then uses additional $0.14x/0.20x/0.26x$ to train ResNet-18/26/34 once after mask transfer. Summing these yields comparable total FLOPs between E-LTH and RigL for the three-model suite, with E-LTH becoming relatively more favorable as the number of target architectures to which the mask transfers increases.
Table2

Present CIFAR-10 DPF comparison data reproduced from the paper (Table 3): for ResNet-20/32/56 at 90% and 95% sparsities, E-LTH matches or slightly improves accuracy drops relative to DPF (dynamic pruning feedback) — for example, ResNet-32 at 90% sparsity shows DPF drop $-1.41\\%$ vs E-LTH drop $-0.96\\%$; in addition, to obtain sparse models across five ResNet variants at the reported sparsities, E-LTH uses a total of $1.26$ billion FLOPs while DPF uses $1.49$ billion FLOPs, indicating E-LTH can be FLOPs-cheaper in aggregate for a suite of targets due to amortization of the one-time IMP cost.
Table3

Explain the FLOPs-normalization and amortization argument used to reach the conclusion: the paper normalizes FLOPs to one dense training pass of ResNet-34 and counts E-LTH's single-source IMP cost once ($2.77x$ in the ImageNet example) plus low per-target training costs for the transferred masks; because DST methods must run separately on each target (e.g., RigL's 5x per-target training), E-LTH becomes cost-competitive or cheaper in total FLOPs when the transferred mask is reused for multiple target architectures.
[11]

Conclude that under FLOPs-normalized, amortized accounting over multiple target architectures, E-LTH (one IMP run plus ETT transfers) attains accuracies comparable to state-of-the-art DST methods (RigL, DPF) while being cost-competitive or cheaper as the number of targets increases, and thus represents a viable cost-accuracy trade-off in multi-target scenarios.

Treat the empirical CIFAR-10 stretching/squeezing ablation experiments as the source of design guidance: the ablation suite used ResNet-32 and ResNet-56 transformations and varied (a) which units are replicated, (b) ordering strategy (appending vs interpolation), and (c) which units are dropped when squeezing, with results averaged over three runs; these ablations are summarized in Figures 4 and 5 and discussed in Section 4.1.
Fig4
Fig5

Rule (a): choose minimal replication units consistent with model structure — for ResNets use residual blocks as the minimal replication unit because blocks are the atomic repeating structure and because residual blocks map naturally to dynamical-systems / unrolled-estimation viewpoints; for VGG use convolution+normalization as the minimal unit. This guideline is explicitly adopted in the ETT implementation and was validated in experiments.
[22]

Rule (b): preserve number of stages, down-sampling blocks, and input/output layers — ablations and the ETT design keep these components invariant to avoid incompatible feature-dimension changes; the paper argues preserving these invariants is essential to produce transferrable masks.

Rule (c): when stretching, prefer replicating more distinct source blocks fewer times (replicate unique units) rather than repeating the same unit many times — the ablation (Figure 4) comparing replicating four distinct blocks vs two distinct blocks vs replicating only the first block shows that replicating more unique units yields better accuracy, and the gap widens at higher sparsities, supporting this heuristic for preserving per-stage sparsity and interpolation-like behavior.
Fig4

Rule (d): replication ordering (appending vs interpolation) yields comparable performance empirically — the paper implements both appending (append replicated blocks after the last original) and interpolation (insert replicated block after its source) and reports similar performance in experiments, so either ordering is acceptable in practice.
Fig2

Rule (e): prefer replicating/dropping later blocks less aggressively and avoid dropping too many early blocks — the ablation in Figure 5 shows that replicating earlier blocks tends to yield better performance at high sparsity and that dropping many early blocks (e.g., the first four) significantly degrades accuracy; additionally, the squeezing experiments reveal ETTs are insensitive to whether dropped blocks are consecutive or non-consecutive so long as early blocks are not excessively removed.
Fig5

Rule (f): these choices matter more at high sparsity levels — across the ablation plots the observed differences between replication/drop strategies are amplified at higher sparsities and smaller at lower sparsities, indicating that adherence to the above heuristics is particularly important when the target mask is very sparse.

Start from ETTs as an available transformation mechanism (established earlier) and test their applicability beyond convolutional residual stacks by designing two kinds of preliminary experiments: (1) transfers involving fully-connected (FC) layers within VGG variants and MLP models (Appendix C), and (2) transfers across dataset shifts and across both architecture and dataset (Appendix D).
Table5

Describe the FC-layer experiments and setup: for VGG variants, vary the number of FC layers on top of convolutional layers (VGG-13-2, VGG-13-3, VGG-13-5) and transfer between these variants; for MLPs on MNIST use MLP-$n$ architectures with hidden-layer widths scaled by $n$; use sparsity ratio $89.26\\%$ for all these experiments and apply ETTs that replicate or drop entire FC layers consistent with the minimal-unit decision used for VGG experiments.
Table5

Report the FC-layer numerical outcomes (from the paper's Table 5): across all VGG-13-2/3/5 and MLP-2/3/4 transfers at $89.26\\%$ sparsity, E-LTH transfers have at most $0.21\\%$ accuracy difference relative to baselines, with example numbers showing VGG and MLP transferred accuracies clustered tightly (e.g., VGG transfers around $93.4\\%-93.6\\%$; MLP transfers around $97.8\\%-98.1\\%$), demonstrating ETTs can handle FC-layer replication/drop without large degradation in these preliminary tests.
Table5

Describe dataset-shift experiments and setup: follow prior work settings for dataset transfer; when only the dataset changes but architecture is the same, directly transfer the winning ticket found by IMP to the new dataset; when both architecture and dataset change, apply ETTs for architecture change (e.g., ResNet-20 source to ResNet-32 target) and transfer across datasets as appropriate; report results averaged as in earlier experiments.
[33]

Report dataset transfer numerical outcomes (from the paper's Table 6 and Appendix D): (a) transferring RN-20 ticket from SVHN to CIFAR-10 and applying ETT to reach RN-32 target yields a target accuracy of $88.67\\%$ versus the IMP baseline $92.22\\%$, a net drop of $3.55\\%$ compared to the IMP baseline; (b) in other dataset/architecture combinations the authors observe that dataset shifts and architecture shifts each cause drops but these drops do not simply add linearly when both are applied; (c) ImageNet→CIFAR-10 transfers (Table 7) show small drops — for example, directly transferring the ResNet-18 ImageNet ticket to CIFAR-10 yields $95.40\\%$ vs IMP $95.42\\%$, effectively almost no drop.
Table6
Table7

Conclude that preliminary experiments show ETTs can transfer winning tickets involving FC layers with small accuracy differences and can be combined with dataset transfer — these tests indicate partial robustness of E-LTH beyond purely convolutional residual stacks, while also noting the observed non-negligible dataset-transfer drops in some cases and recommending further study.

Treat ETTs (mapping functions) and the CIFAR-10 experimental evidence of their high-quality transfers (conclusions 2 and 3) as established premises for studying mode connectivity; apply the linear interpolation test used in prior work to measure linear mode connectivity: train two independent instances (different SGD noise/augmentations) of the same ticket and measure the test accuracy along linear interpolations between the two trained parameter vectors, observing whether interpolation retains comparable accuracy to the endpoints.
[14]

Describe the specific linear-mode-connectivity experiment the paper ran: take IMP-found winning tickets trained independently on the same target (ResNet-32) and measure interpolation stability (IMP baseline); take ETT-transferred tickets derived from ResNet-14→ResNet-32 and ResNet-20→ResNet-32 and train them independently, then measure maximal accuracy drop along linear interpolations between two independently trained copies for each transfer source; plot interpolation accuracy vs interpolation coefficient to observe degradation patterns (this is the experimental protocol summarized in the paper and illustrated in Figure 8).
Fig8

Report the observed interpolation stability numbers (from Figure 8): the IMP-found tickets are observed to be stable under linear interpolation (little to no accuracy degradation across interpolation), ETTs transferred from ResNet-20 to ResNet-32 incur a maximal interpolation accuracy drop of $8.72\\%$, whereas ETTs transferred from ResNet-14 to ResNet-32 incur a much larger maximal interpolation drop of $69.72\\%$. These quantitative gaps show ETT-transferred tickets' linear connectivity degrades with increasing source-target depth difference.
Fig8

Conclude that ETT-transferred tickets can preserve linear mode connectivity properties similar to IMP-found winning tickets when the source and target are close in depth (smaller depth gap), but this connectivity stability degrades as the depth difference increases; thus ETTs better preserve linear connectivity when the source and target likely reside in the same loss basin (smaller depth gap), consistent with the paper's assertion that transfer success is correlated with staying in the same basin.

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges multiple unresolved scientific issues and limitations for future work: (1) scope limitation — current E-LTH/ETTs focus on depth transformations within a single design family; extending transferability to width changes, mixed topological transformations, or transfers across disparate families remains unresolved and is empirically challenging (width transforms were found to be much harder in preliminary attempts). (2) theoretical understanding — current rationales (dynamical-systems and unrolled estimation perspectives) are preliminary hypotheses restricted largely to ResNets; rigorous theory explaining when and why a source ticket's sparse mask remains trainable after replication/dropping is not established. (3) structured sparsity — producing high-quality structured (e.g., channel) winning tickets that are hardware-friendly remains open; most LTH/ETT work here is unstructured. (4) general criteria of "architectural similarity" — a precise definition of which architectures belong to the same transferable design family and how to measure that similarity (beyond repeating blocks and stage counts) is unresolved. (5) basin identification and transfer limits — understanding loss-basin relationships that determine whether a transferred ticket will land in the same basin as target-IMP tickets, and characterizing safe depth/transform ranges for reliable transfer, are open. Addressing these questions is required to generalize E-LTH beyond the present, depth-oriented, same-family regime and to provide principled guidance for broader, automated ticket transfer.
